# The Training Schedule Can Create an ACWR to Injury Association Without ACWR Causing Injury

**What it is** — The speakers (Luke Bourne, caption spelling, and Patrick Ward) propose a causal structure, drawn as a directed acyclic graph (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:10]). The published analyses compute ACWR going into each session and check whether an injury occurred in that session (TIRINmtZOu0 [10:10], [10:40]). The speakers add a missing third variable: the schedule drives both ACWR and the intensity of the upcoming session, and session intensity drives injury (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:10], [11:41]). If the last seven days were hard, ACWR is high, and the next session is also likely to be hard (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:41]). Their density plots show that when athletes are in the "danger zone" of ACWR, upcoming session loads are higher than when they are in the "sweet spot" (TIRINmtZOu0 [16:16], [16:47]). Schedule features named: training camp, where load jumps from zero to a lot, international breaks, and the weekly cycle (TIRINmtZOu0 [09:39], [16:47], [17:18]). They open with an ice cream and drowning example of confounding (TIRINmtZOu0 [03:33]).

**Why it works** — The structure is a standard confounder: a shared cause makes two variables move together. The speakers show two things: the simulation in [[claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect]], and that in their real data the ACWR association goes from "highly significant to non-significant" once same-session load is accounted for, in all their cases (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19], [18:49]). The adjusted effect sizes and models are "in the paper" and were not shown (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]). The speakers give no physiological mechanism for why session intensity raises injury risk; they treat it as given. Inference: a high-intensity session in itself being the injury exposure is consistent with how they frame it, but the talk does not test it.

**When to apply** — Whenever a load metric computed from the days before a session is correlated with an outcome in that session. Inference: check whether the metric also predicts the load of the session itself; if it does, the metric may be a proxy for that load. Eric's baseline (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred): abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver, and progressions are kept smooth. The talk does not contradict this: it says the ratio may reflect the schedule and leaves open whether spikes themselves cause injury.

**When NOT to apply** — Contested. This is the speakers' explanation, supported by one simulation and unshown real-data adjustments from two teams. The speakers themselves say they have not disproved the earlier papers and that the explanation is "another really good explanation" (TIRINmtZOu0 [19:19]). Existing library: Griffin 2020, a systematic review of 22 studies, reports ACWR associations with non-contact injury and recommends use inside a broader multifactorial monitoring system, so it does not read the association as pure artifact; Impellizzeri 2020 agrees with the artifact reading on Serie A data. Whether chronic load is protective is explicitly not addressed (TIRINmtZOu0 [26:42]). Do not use this entry to claim that training load is irrelevant to injury.

**Example** — The speakers' own: training camp, where coaches "purposefully increase training demands" and where the literature also finds the highest injury risk, raises ACWR and session intensity together (TIRINmtZOu0 [09:39]).

**Related** — [[framework--null-model-simulation-to-test-a-risk-metric]]; [[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]; [[claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]] (agrees); [[research-papers/griffin-2020-the-association-between-the-acute-chronic-workload-ratio-and-injury-and-its-application-in]] (the association literature, disagrees in emphasis); [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-training-load-and-injury-part-2-questionable-research-practices-hijack-the-truth-and-misle]].

They also report that acute load alone gave the same results as the ratio, and that coupled and uncoupled denominators gave the same results (TIRINmtZOu0 [26:42]).

**When to apply** — When building or auditing an injury model on load data with session-level records. Inference: a first pass is to compare a model with the prior-load ratio alone against the same model plus today's planned session load. The speaker notes the approach needs "a fair bit of statistical" skill and that much of the original literature came from people whose background was not statistical (TIRINmtZOu0 [25:11], [25:41]). Two teams, two sports.

**Example** — Inference: for a non-contact hamstring injury in a Tuesday practice, the record would hold the Tuesday session's planned intensity next to the prior-week ratio; the model asks whether the ratio adds anything once Tuesday's intensity is in.

# Keep the Load Record of the Session in Which an Injury Occurs

**What it is** — The speaker (Luke Bourne, caption spelling) says earlier studies did not use same-session load for a simple reason: when a player is injured mid-session, that session's data is "censored" or thrown out. His example is that nobody is going to "carefully extract the GPS unit" in the middle of the field during an NFL practice (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:18], [17:49]). The result is that the analysis sees load before the injury session but not the intensity of the session itself, which is the variable the speakers argue matters most (see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]). The heuristic: make sure the injured session's load, or at minimum its planned intensity, is saved.

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is about missing data, not physiology: without the session's own load, a model cannot separate it from the prior-load ratio. The speaker gives no figure for how much data is lost. Inference: an injured athlete's device often stops mid-session, so the partial record can still carry the load up to the injury.

**When to apply** — Whenever the department logs injuries against GPS or session data. Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack, with a documented session lifecycle and data cleaning with spike detection (Explicit, Playbook p.7, pp.9-11). Inference: the cleaning step, or a missing export after an early stop, is the place where an injured session could be dropped; check that the partial session is retained and flagged. A practical first check: count how many non-contact injuries have a recorded session load for the day of injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speaker's assertion about common practice in the literature, not a measured loss rate, and it comes from the NFL and European soccer. It does not by itself fix the confounding; the model adjustment is a separate step ([[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]). Contact injuries are outside the speakers' definition, which is a non-contact injury that makes the player miss a subsequent session or match, in line with the UEFA definition (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22], [20:53]); the speaker also says an off-field injury cannot be ruled out as training-related (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a player injured in the middle of an NFL practice, where "the last thing they're worried about" is capturing the GPS data (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]].

# Daily Wellness Questionnaires Often Collapse to the Same Number

**What it is** — In the Q&A, one speaker says the injury and training relationship is a dose and response relationship, and that team sport has no great measure of response. Wellness questionnaires are "a good idea," but he has "never seen any good validation," and in "four different sports" over "years of data" the data are "essentially a bunch of professional athletes putting the number seven in every day" (TIRINmtZOu0 [24:39]). The caption says "seven"; the scale is not stated. The speaker is not identified in the captions between the two presenters. He also says dose is measurable and response is not well measured (TIRINmtZOu0 [24:06], [24:39]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for why athletes enter one value. Inference: a repeated low-effort answer is the quickest way to finish a daily form, and nothing about the answer is checked against an outcome.

**When to apply** — As a check before putting a subjective wellness item into a multivariate injury or readiness model: look at the within-athlete variance first. Inference: if most athletes' entries barely move across weeks, the item cannot carry a signal. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys rolled out across sports in summer 2022 were abandoned after about one academic year because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers, and wellness surveys are still used in return-to-play and chronic-health cases (Explicit, SportSmith piece, 2026-02-19). The speaker's observation matches Eric's reason for dropping them.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one speaker's experience across four sports, not a study, and no values, sample size or teams are given. It is not a statement that all subjective monitoring fails; the same speaker says wellness, physiological and biomarker data in a multivariate model might do better (TIRINmtZOu0 [23:35], [24:06]). Professional athletes are the stated population; a college roster with different incentives may behave differently.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the number "seven" entered every day by professional athletes, across four sports and years of data (TIRINmtZOu0 [24:39]).

**Related** — [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]] (the same Q&A, on whether richer data could replace the ratio). Existing library: [[research-papers/rebelo-2026-monitoring-training-effects-in-athletes-a-multidimensional-framework-for-decision-making]] (multidimensional monitoring).

# Frame Lineup Selection as a Sequential Decision: Markov Decision Process Solved by Monte Carlo Tree Search

**What it is** — The presenter (Ryan Beiel, caption spelling, CEO of the startup Sentient Sports) and the lead author (Greg Everett, caption spelling, in recorded video segments) describe a framework for choosing a soccer starting eleven that balances winning now against injury risk later (K5a7C4b1Cwc [00:00], [01:31], [02:01]). Each week: a team plans its upcoming matches; every player has a skill rating and a next-match injury probability, both from separate models; an optimization picks the 11 starters; the state updates for injuries that occurred and for player use; repeat week after week (K5a7C4b1Cwc [02:01], [02:31]). The coach's problem is framed as a Markov decision process (MDP) whose objective is to maximize expected points over the season while balancing the chance of winning upcoming matches against injury risk to key players (K5a7C4b1Cwc [06:37]). Because the decision space is large, they approximate the optimum with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS). Nodes are MDP states (current match, player injury risks, existing injuries), branches are team selections, and leaf nodes are the next match with updated injuries (K5a7C4b1Cwc [07:07]). The loop: selection by an upper confidence bound heuristic, expansion by "progressive broadening," simulation of the rest of the season assuming the coach picks the most qualified team, and back-propagation of expected points to the root (K5a7C4b1Cwc [07:38], [08:09], [08:39]). It repeats thousands or millions of times and returns the selection with the highest expected value (K5a7C4b1Cwc [08:39]).

**Why it works** — The speakers' argument is that a greedy choice each week ignores the later cost of an injury, while the tree search values future matches (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12]). Their stated expectation is that resting a player lowers workload and so injury risk, if the rest is timed so that performance is not sacrificed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). The speakers give no evidence in the talk that rest at a given moment lowers a specific player's risk beyond what their injury model assumes. Inference: the framework is only as good as the injury-probability model feeding it; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]].

**When to apply** — As a design pattern for any roster-rotation question where today's choice changes tomorrow's availability (rest rotation, minutes management). Inference: the pieces that transfer are the separation of three parts (a per-player availability or injury model, a per-lineup performance model, and a search over sequences) and the explicit horizon; see [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]]. Eric's baseline: football has an in-season game-week structure (Sunday off, Monday heavy lift, hard practice ending 72 hours before a Saturday game, interview 2026-09-28, Q15, Explicit) and a bye-week rule that players with few snaps practice harder (Q17, Explicit); rest decisions are made by schedule design and coach judgment, not by a search model.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested outside simulation. The presenter says it is a framework built on free and open data, not a medical prediction tool, no club has used it, and a team would have to be convinced to follow it (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48], [18:54]). Resting is all or nothing for a full match; substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). It was tested on Premier League data only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18], [19:54]). American football, with large rosters, position-specific roles, contact injuries and no free rotation, is named only as future work (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15], [14:18]). The speaker has a startup interest in the method.

**Example** — The speakers' own: for N'Golo Kante, the model kept his predicted injury probability low through the season except the final stretch, where the real Chelsea rested him and the model chose to start him (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]). A single example, shown as an illustration.

**Related** — [[framework--adapt-maher-expected-points-model-with-player-skill]]; [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]; [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]]. # Make a Team-Level Match Model Sensitive to the Starting Eleven

**What it is** — The reward in the team-selection framework is expected points for a match. The presenters (Ryan Beiel and, in recorded video, the lead author Greg Everett, caption spellings) compute it from an adapted Maher model (caption "Maya"), a common soccer prediction model that assumes each team's scoring rate follows a Poisson distribution and learns offensive and defensive strengths from historical data to get win, draw and loss probabilities (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:05]). The original model works at team level and ignores individual selections, so they replaced the team-identity features with player-based numerical features: a player contribution model (caption "VAPE", likely a value-of-actions style model, not confirmed) supplies each player's skill value, and the combined skills of the chosen eleven feed a linear model (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:36], [06:06]). The output is converted to expected points per match, which also shows how important each match is to the season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [02:31], [06:06]). They report that over two Premier League seasons the adapted model achieved "similar performance, within the margins of error," to the original, with added flexibility to measure outcomes for individual selections (K5a7C4b1Cwc [06:06]).

**Why it works** — Replacing team identity with the skills of the named eleven lets the model respond to who plays, which is what a rest decision changes. The speakers give no numbers for the comparison (no error metric or margins shown in captions), so the equivalence to the original model is a statement, not a result you can cite. Inference: matching the original within error means the adaptation did not lose predictive power at team level; it does not show the player-level contributions are accurate.

**When to apply** — When a decision model needs a performance term that changes with the lineup. Inference: the check to copy is the one the speakers describe, comparing the adapted model against the original team-level model on held-out seasons before using it as a reward.

**When NOT to apply** — Two Premier League seasons, StatsBomb event data for 2017/18 and 2018/19 (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11]). Soccer scoring is Poisson-like, which is the model's central assumption; do not carry the form to American football scoring without checking. The player skill model's name and construction are garbled in the captions, so the skill values cannot be reproduced from this talk. Untested in this library: no comparison numbers are available.

**Example** — The speakers' own: slide jerseys carrying numerical skill values for each player of a team, summed into the starting eleven's strength for a match (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:36], [06:06]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]].

# In a Soccer Injury Model, Short- and Long-Term Workload and Detailed Injury History Mattered Most

**What it is** — The presenters report a gradient-boosted tree injury model (caption "XG boost") trained on injury-related features built from 2017-18 Premier League data and a historical career injury dataset (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). Inputs per player and match include workload from earlier selections, injury history (age, number of injuries) and context such as opponent and travel distance (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]). Using SHAP values, the least important group was contextual: travel to the game and rain. The next group, with somewhat more weight: days since the last injury, match-day temperature and age. The group that contributed most: the player's workload across matches, both short and long term, and the player's detailed injury history (K5a7C4b1Cwc [04:03], [04:33]). Testing: a 70/30 split with "five-block" cross-validation (caption spelling, probably five-fold), log loss 0.16, outperforming other base models tried (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [09:42]); a Pearson correlation of 0.77 between the model's predictions and the 2018/19 Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). The talk does not say what was correlated (it reads as predicted versus observed injury outcomes) and gives no number of injuries or players.

**Why it works** — The speakers give no mechanism for why workload and injury history dominate; they report the SHAP ranking. Inference: prior injuries and recent load are the two inputs most directly tied to a specific player's tissue state, while travel and weather are shared across a squad.

**When to apply** — As a prior for what to log first when building an injury model with limited data: workload at more than one time scale, and a detailed injury history. Eric's baseline: there is no formal injury-risk model, and movement screens are collected and filed without changing programs (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit); this model's top inputs are workload and history, not screens.

**When NOT to apply** — Player load was imputed from event data by a separate model, because tracking data is not open (K5a7C4b1Cwc [17:53]); there was no club medical data and no training load, so the workload feature misses training exposure, which a questioner pressed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:24], [18:54]). One league, two seasons, soccer, professional players. The presenter says it is a decision framework, "not an expert medical prediction model" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:54]). A correlation of 0.77 and a log loss of 0.16 are reported without class balance, so how the model would rank athletes in practice is unknown. Existing library caution: ACWR-style workload features carry the confounding concern in [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]], which this model's authors do not address.

**Example** — The speakers' own: for a player facing Watford, the model takes his workload from the previous selections, his injury history and age, and the opponent and travel distance, and outputs an injury probability for that match (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]] (workload-ratio confounding, contested). Existing library: [[research-papers/carey-2017-predictive-modelling-of-training-loads-and-injury-in-australian-football]].

# Simulated Result: Tree-Search Selection Cut Injuries at Similar Expected Points

**What it is** — The presenters compared their search-based selection with a greedy baseline that picks the team maximizing expected points for each match only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42], [10:12]). They ran thousands of simulations per season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:43], [11:14]). Reported: Brighton would have benefited most, with 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least, with 7.5% fewer in the ideal eleven; across all Premier League teams on average, 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal starting eleven, with similar expected points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14], [11:44]). The headline at the end, "approximately 13% on average" fewer injuries, matches the ideal-eleven figure, not the 4.6% squad figure, and the speaker does not say which (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]). Compared with real coaches, the search model's selections were about 76% similar and the greedy model's about 82%; the presenters suggest managers face short-term pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43]). They also say real technical directors often decide for short-term gains over long-term athlete protection (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:48]); this is stated as a belief, with no survey of directors shown.

**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that the search values future availability and the greedy rule does not. They give no mechanism beyond the injury model's workload dependence; see [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]. Inference: because both models use the same injury model to score the outcome, the comparison measures how the injury model's own risk estimates change selections, not real injuries.

**When to apply** — As an illustration of what a rest-rotation decision model might claim, and of the size of benefit a vendor or paper could be expected to show. Inference: a claim of fewer injuries from a model should come with the injury model's validation, which this talk gives only partly (log loss 0.16, Pearson 0.77; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: all results are simulated from open data (StatsBomb 2017/18 and 2018/19 Premier League events, Transfermarkt injury history), with player load imputed and no club medical or training data (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [13:48], [17:53]). No club has used the recommendations, and sample size beyond two seasons is not stated. Substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). One league, professional soccer; do not apply the percentages to college football, where rotation is far more limited. The speaker has a startup interest. The 13% versus 4.6% ambiguity above means the headline should be quoted with both figures.

**Example** — The speakers' own: Brighton, 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven at similar points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--injury-risk-multiplier-robustness]]; [[claim--modeled-wage-savings-from-fewer-injuries]]; [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]].

# Stress Test: With Injury Risk Two and Three Times Higher, the Search Model Gained Points and Injury Savings Shrank

**What it is** — To test robustness in higher-risk settings "not seen in our test data" (an intense run of cup matches, or contact sports such as rugby or American football), the presenters multiplied standard injury risks by two and three and again compared the search model with the greedy baseline (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:44], [12:15]). Reported: in higher-risk scenarios the search model outperformed the greedy model on season performance, with a 1.8% increase in expected points when risk was three times higher (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15]). As injury probability rose, the margin of injury reduction over the greedy baseline shrank, which they attribute to the strategy being forced into certain choices by multiple injuries, though injuries still fell "significantly" across all multipliers (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15], [12:46]). The talk gives no injury-reduction percentages for the 2x and 3x cases.

**Why it works** — The presenter's own explanation for the shrinking margin is forced decisions when many players are out; no further mechanism is given. Inference: when the available pool is thin, there is less room to rest anyone, so selection differences between the two rules narrow.

**When to apply** — As a reading aid for any rotation model: ask whether the benefit holds when risk is raised, and whether the injury margin shrinks as roster depth thins. Inference: for a football roster with positional depth limits, the shrinking-margin pattern is the more relevant half of this result.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a scaled version of a soccer injury model, not data from rugby or American football; the presenters list those sports as future work (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15], [14:18]). Multiplying risk by 2 or 3 assumes the same feature relationships hold at higher risk, which is not tested. No numbers beyond 1.8% are given, and it is a simulated result with no external validation. Do not cite it as evidence that the method works in contact sports.

**Example** — The speakers' own: injury risk at three times the standard level, search model 1.8% more expected points than greedy (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15]).

**Related** — [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]; [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]].

# Plan Rest Over a Rolling Horizon, Not Just the Next Match

**What it is** — Two points from the talk. First, the greedy rule of picking the best team for each match ignores long-term injury and absence risk, and the presenters found real coaches' selections closer to the greedy model (82% similar) than to their search model (76%), which they attribute to short-term job pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43], [14:48]). Second, in the Q&A, a questioner (not named) compared it to an American "survivor pool" in which picking the best matchups early corners you later, and suggested optimizing only the next X games and re-optimizing as injuries occur and player skill estimates change (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49], [16:20]). The presenter replied that the model has a parameter for how many games forward to simulate, from the end of the season to a five-game window moved forward week by week (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:51]).

**Why it works** — The speakers' stated reason is that rest taken now has a payoff in later matches, and a short window lets the coach re-plan with real information on who is available (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:20]). The presenter gives no result comparing a five-game window with a full-season horizon. Inference: a shorter horizon trades some foresight for robustness to model error, since injury and skill estimates drift.

**When to apply** — When planning rest or playing time across a congested stretch: set an explicit horizon (for example, the next several games), re-plan each week with updated availability, and name what the greedy option would be so the cost of the short-term choice is visible. Eric's baseline: in football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason the priority window (interview 2026-09-28, Q14, Explicit), and bye weeks give players with few snaps harder practice (Q17, Explicit). Inference: those are horizon decisions already made by calendar, and the heuristic asks whether any are made match by match instead.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the horizon parameter is described, not evaluated, and the greedy-versus-search similarity numbers come from one league's open data (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [10:12]). The explanation of coaches' choices (job pressure) is the presenters' belief. In football the roster and the game schedule give one game a week and no free rotation, so the "next X games" horizon is short already.

**Example** — The questioner's own analogy: a survivor-pool player who uses all the best teams early has nothing left late in the season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]].

# Sleep Deficits Accumulate, and Three Nights of Recovery Sleep Do Not Fully Erase Them

**What it is** — The speaker, a sleep scientist (unnamed in the captions) who refers to her lab at Henry Ford, says that getting six to seven hours instead of eight "doubles or triples" normal reaction time, which she puts at about a quarter of a second (J7smyg1Czik [01:33]). She shows a sleep deprivation study in which the same individuals go through different conditions: seven days of restricted time in bed (the captions give "7 five versus 3 hours", garbled) versus nine hours in bed, each followed by three days of nine-hour recovery sleep (J7smyg1Czik [02:05], [02:36]). Mean speed and the number of lapses worsened as days of deficit increased; after three recovery days at nine hours in bed, the restricted group recovered but "never as good as" people who get nine hours regularly (J7smyg1Czik [02:36]). She concludes that deficits are cumulative and "non-recoverable" over a short window, so sleep before a game is not enough (J7smyg1Czik [22:33]), and says athletes tend to sleep poorly right before games because of anxiety or a strange environment (J7smyg1Czik [03:07]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for accumulation; she shows the study result. Inference: the result as stated means a short recovery block does not return performance to the level of consistently well-rested people, so the amount of regular sleep leading up to an event matters more than the last night.

**When to apply** — When advising athletes before a competition or travel block: focus on sleep across the preceding days, not only the night before. Inference: this supports looking at multi-night sleep, if it were measured. Eric's baseline: recovery is managed through training-load design alone and nothing objective is tracked, sleep included (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). The talk's finding would need some sleep measure to act on; none exists in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — The study's sample size, population, exact restriction and test are not stated, and the design numbers are garbled in the captions. "Non-recoverable" is the speaker's wording for a three-day test; the talk does not follow recovery beyond three days. Auto-caption talk from 2017; the results were presented by a speaker with a sleep-lab affiliation, not as a peer-reviewed table. It does not apply as a measurement tool: it shows an effect in healthy adults under restriction, not a sleep target for Baylor athletes.

**Example** — The speaker's own: restricted-time-in-bed participants after three nine-hour recovery nights compared with participants who had nine hours throughout (J7smyg1Czik [02:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-extension-improved-stanford-athlete-performance]]; [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]] (NCAA Division I sleep and nap behavior).

# Extending Time in Bed to Ten Hours for Six Weeks Improved Stanford Athletes' Performance

**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) summarizes the Stanford sleep-extension studies: athletes were given 10 hours in bed for six weeks, wore actigraphs, kept sleep diaries, and were tested near the end of the six weeks (J7smyg1Czik [09:12], [09:42]). Reported results: basketball players had a significant reduction in sprint times and a 9% increase in both free throws and three-point field goals, were less sleepy, and rated their mood better (J7smyg1Czik [09:42], [10:13]); football players shaved time off the 40-yard dash and the 20-yard shuttle (the caption reads "1 point1 2 seconds", garbled, so the amount is not confirmed) (J7smyg1Czik [10:13], [10:44]); swimmers improved average turn time and added "five kicks" to their strokes (caption wording, unclear) (J7smyg1Czik [11:14]); tennis players improved serve accuracy (J7smyg1Czik [11:14]). From these she says adults need 7 to 8 hours but athletes need 9 to 10 (J7smyg1Czik [08:42], [09:12], [11:14]). The 9 to 10 hour figure is her synthesis of these studies, not a stated finding of any one of them. In the Q&A she acknowledges the extension studies measured time in bed, not sleep (J7smyg1Czik [25:57]).

**Why it works** — The speaker connects the gains to the effects listed earlier in her talk (reaction time, judgment, mood) but gives no direct mechanism for these results. Inference: the improvements may come from reduced chronic sleep loss in athletes who started short, not from sleeping more than needed; the talk does not report baseline sleep.

**When to apply** — As background when an athlete group is plainly short on sleep and the schedule allows more time in bed (for example, no early-morning facility constraints). Inference: this supports aiming to enable more time in bed before aiming at a specific hour target. Eric's baseline: sleep is not tracked and recovery is managed through training-load design alone (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). The speaker also says sports limited by facility times, such as swimming and ice hockey, are hit hardest (J7smyg1Czik [23:55]).

**When NOT to apply** — Sample sizes, effect sizes (beyond the 9% shooting figures) and statistics are not given, and no control group is described in the talk. Time in bed was extended, so quality and total sleep were not measured. The athletes are Stanford athletes in four sports; there is no football-position, no NFL and no Baylor data. The 9 to 10 hours target should not be read as a requirement: the speaker says individual need varies in the Q&A (J7smyg1Czik [26:58]). A 2017 conference talk with no stated citation for the studies.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Stanford basketball players with a 9% increase in free throws and in three-point field goals after six weeks of 10 hours in bed (J7smyg1Czik [09:42]).

# Circadian Timing Changed Game Results: West Coast Evening NFL Teams and East Coast Baseball Teams

**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) lays out a general premise: physiological functions that affect performance, such as best coordination, fastest reaction time, greatest cardiovascular efficiency and muscle strength, tend to peak in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [13:49]). Evidence she cites for games. NFL: "my colleagues Smith and motra" (caption spelling) examined 40 years of NFL data on evening games between East Coast and West Coast teams, and found the West Coast beat the Las Vegas point spread and won "twice as often," with no significant difference in daytime games (J7smyg1Czik [14:19], [14:49]). She calls it robust, and says it accounts for team quality and travel, so the homeostatic (time awake) drive does not explain it (J7smyg1Czik [14:49], [15:20]). Baseball: a study about five or six years before her talk (J7smyg1Czik [15:20]) found that crossing three time zones raised the chance of losing the first game, "60% or more" in the captions (unclear); and that East Coast teams returning home lost their home advantage, about 3.9%, when playing away teams from the same time zone (J7smyg1Czik [15:50], [16:20]). She also says morning-type pitchers pitch better in day games and night-type pitchers in evening games (J7smyg1Czik [15:50]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that every physiological function has a circadian rhythm and each body's clock peaks at a time of day; a team playing at its own biological peak has an advantage (J7smyg1Czik [13:49], [14:49]). She treats the NFL result as the circadian effect alone because the analysis controls for travel and team quality. Her description of the controls is brief.

**When to apply** — As a scheduling consideration for evening games and travel across time zones. Inference: for a team that travels across time zones for a game, this supports timing meals, sleep and training to the local clock where the schedule allows. Eric's baseline: no sleep or travel monitoring beyond training-load design is in the baseline (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit); the game-week structure is set by the Saturday game (Q15, Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — The NFL study is described by the speaker; its method is not shown beyond "controls for team quality and travel," and the authors are caption-spelled. The baseball numbers are garbled in the captions ("60% or more" and 3.9% are unclear whether they are probabilities, percent changes or percentage points). NFL evening games are professional, with specific travel patterns; college football kickoff times, travel and east-west mixes differ and were not studied. The result is about averages across teams and does not tell you which individual players are affected. Existing library guidance on athlete sleep and jet lag is an expert consensus, not a game-outcomes study.

**Example** — The speaker's own: West Coast teams winning evening games against East Coast teams about twice as often, with no difference in daytime games, over 40 years (J7smyg1Czik [14:19], [14:49]).

# Classify Chronotype, Then Time Peak Performance Relative to When the Athlete Wakes

**What it is** — A method the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) describes from a study she attributes to a "university of Birmingham" (caption spelling) group. Competition-level athletes completed a paper-and-pencil morning-evening questionnaire, which classified them as early, intermediate or late (night owl) (J7smyg1Czik [17:22], [17:52]). Performance tests were done six times across the day: the bleep test (endurance, oxygen uptake) and sprint times, along with athletes' own ratings (J7smyg1Czik [17:52], [18:24]). As a whole group, performance was lowest at 7 am and highest in the late afternoon; the captions read "between four and seven" without am or pm (J7smyg1Czik [18:24], [18:55]). By chronotype, early types peaked between noon and 2, intermediate types in the mid-afternoon, and late types between 7 and 8 in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [18:55]). Relative to waking, early and intermediate types peaked about 6 to 7 hours after waking, and late types 11 hours or more after (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). A further analysis of a large number of athletes in 12 teams predicted team peak by team makeup: a team of mostly late types (T3) peaked later than a team of mostly early types (T10) (J7smyg1Czik [20:30], [21:00]). In the Q&A she says the body clock shifts mostly with light and can be moved with light boxes and melatonin, for example earlier bedtimes for a team trip to London, and that this takes discipline (J7smyg1Czik [29:02]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a biological clock decides whether someone is a night owl or morning lark, and everyone's peak therefore differs (J7smyg1Czik [16:51], [17:22]). Her point is that a fixed wake time, imposed by a coach or schedule, does not shift when an individual peaks (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). She gives no mechanism for the questionnaire's validity.

**When to apply** — When choosing the time of day for testing or high-stakes sessions, or when comparing an athlete's results across times. Inference: record each athlete's test time and, if the staff wishes, the questionnaire result, before comparing sessions; this matters for repeatable testing. Eric's baseline (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred): testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). Eric's baseline: Eric has no stated chronotype practice; the baseline is silent.

**When NOT to apply** — Sample sizes are not stated for the questionnaire study; the only count is 12 teams. The study is competition-level athletes, not college football, and early-morning football practice and meal schedules are not under athletes' control. The speaker says the whole circadian advantage is "unexplored" (J7smyg1Czik [22:33], [23:03]). Her claim that a third of teams she talks to are not interested is her own experience (J7smyg1Czik [28:31]). A light and melatonin protocol was mentioned, not described; do not use it as a medical recommendation.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Team 3, mostly late types, versus Team 10, mostly early types; she says if a morning game pitted them against each other, T3 would be at a biological disadvantage, and in the evening T10 would be (J7smyg1Czik [21:00], [21:32]).

**Related** — [[claim--circadian-misalignment-shifts-game-outcomes-nfl-and-baseball]]; [[heuristic--strategic-nap-lengths-and-when-not-to-nap]].

# If an Athlete Sleeps In on Days Off, Treat It as a Sign of a Weekday Deficit

**What it is** — In the Q&A, asked how to tell who needs eight hours and who nine, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says two things. First, people who say they can get by on five to seven hours are not people who need less; they tolerate deprivation better (J7smyg1Czik [26:58], [27:29]). Second, chronic deprivation makes you "lose your reference" for what being awake and alert feels like, so people think they are fine on five or six hours and never extend their sleep (J7smyg1Czik [27:29], [28:00]). Her check: find out whether the person sleeps in on days off or weekends, because that means they are not getting enough sleep on a regular basis and are "playing catch up" (J7smyg1Czik [28:00]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that sleeping in is the body repaying a debt, and a person with a debt cannot rate their own alertness reliably. This is her assertion, with no study cited. Inference: because self-report is the problem, a behavioral sign (extra sleep on free days) is a more reliable cue than asking "do you feel rested."

**When to apply** — As a cheap screening question for athletes with fatigue complaints, poor test results or high injury concern: ask what time they wake on days off compared with training days. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were abandoned because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers (Explicit, SportSmith piece, 2026-02-19), and nothing objective is tracked for sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). Inference: a one-time behavioral question is a different data type from a daily scale and avoids the same gaming problem, but that is untested.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: no data supporting the weekend-sleep cue are shown in the talk. Athletes may sleep in for reasons other than debt (an illness, a late game, travel). A talk speaker's rule of thumb should not replace a clinical evaluation of sleep problems, and the speaker herself separates sleep need from tolerance without giving a way to measure need. College athletes' days off are set by schedule and may not reflect free choice.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a person who says they need only five or six hours but sleeps in at the weekend, which she reads as a regular deficit (J7smyg1Czik [27:29], [28:00]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[claim--sleep-extension-improved-stanford-athlete-performance]]; [[claim--wellness-questionnaires-collapse-to-one-number]] (why self-report scales fail). # Strategic Naps: 15 to 20 Minutes, 30 Minutes or 90 Minutes, and Not When Night Sleep Is Poor

**What it is** — In the Q&A, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says nine hours in bed means nine hours over a 24-hour period, so an athlete who cannot sleep it all at once can nap (J7smyg1Czik [29:33]). Her caution: if the athlete has trouble sleeping at night, a nap is "not a good thing," because it uses up the homeostatic sleep drive (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). She also says trouble falling asleep in athletes usually comes from trying to sleep at an unusual time after crossing time zones (the example is four) or from heavy caffeine in the evening because games are in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). She adds that napping after training helps, since sleep consolidates learning and memory formed in training (J7smyg1Czik [25:25]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism for the length choice is the sleep stage you wake from: light sleep in the short naps, a full cycle in the 90-minute nap. Her caution rests on sleep drive (time awake) opposing sleep, as she describes it earlier in the talk (J7smyg1Czik [11:45], [12:48]). No study is cited for the nap lengths.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's schedule leaves time in bed short, and nighttime sleep is otherwise good. Inference: the three lengths give a short and a long option for a travel day or a long gap between sessions. Eric's baseline: no sleep or nap protocol is in the baseline; recovery is managed through training-load design alone (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the nap guidance is the speaker's practical advice with no data, population or study cited. Not for athletes with poor night sleep (her own rule). A 90-minute nap before a session may cause grogginess; the talk does not address timing relative to training or competition. Not a substitute for a clinical sleep evaluation. Naps are a make-up for total sleep, not a replacement for regular nights, since she says deficits are cumulative (J7smyg1Czik [22:33]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: for an athlete who cannot get nine hours in one go, split it across a night and a nap, choosing the nap length by whether the athlete will have time to wake fully (J7smyg1Czik [29:33], [30:03]).

# Sleep Restriction Lowered Testosterone by 10 to 12% in Young Men, the Speaker Says

**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says growth hormone is secreted in deep sleep and testosterone is secreted while sleeping (with another peak while awake) (J7smyg1Czik [05:40]). She describes an experiment in which young healthy college students had five fewer hours than eight in bed, and their testosterone levels fell by 10 to 12% (the captions read "increased... decreased", so the direction is inferred from the following sentence) (J7smyg1Czik [05:40], [06:12]). Normal aging loss is 1 to 2% per year, so she says a 20-year-old after a week of restriction would look like a 31-year-old (J7smyg1Czik [06:12]). She adds that sleep loss raises the hormones that break down muscle (J7smyg1Czik [06:42]). Related items from her talk: less sleep made people more sensitive to pain in studies from the Henry Ford sleep lab (J7smyg1Czik [06:42], [07:12]); University of Chicago students lost about 40% of glucose tolerance after a week or ten days of restriction (J7smyg1Czik [07:12], [07:42]); and she compares impairment from sleep loss to alcohol, six hours like two to three beers, four hours like about six beers (J7smyg1Czik [07:42], [08:12]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that the hormones are released in sleep, so less sleep means less of them. She names no study authors for any of these results. Inference: a reduction of 10 to 12% in a one-week laboratory restriction of young men says little about an athlete's day-to-day testosterone.

**When to apply** — As background for why sleep is mentioned alongside recovery and hormones, never as a clinical test. Inference: the finding supports asking about sleep when an athlete reports poor recovery. Eric's baseline: nothing objective is tracked for recovery or sleep (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit); no hormone testing is in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: unnamed studies, sample sizes and durations not stated, and the caption garble in the key sentence. College students, mostly or only young men, in laboratory conditions. Existing library: a 2026 review of testosterone in athletes notes that sleep loss and sleep-disordered breathing may contribute to impaired testosterone regulation, and that evidence for sleep extension or melatonin as testosterone-enhancing interventions is not established, so do not present this as a treatment effect. The "age 31" comparison and the alcohol equivalence are the speaker's illustrations, not findings she cites. Do not use this to interpret an athlete's own lab values.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a 20-year-old player after a week of lost sleep, with testosterone like that of a 31-year-old (J7smyg1Czik [06:12]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[claim--sleep-hours-predicted-injury-in-high-school-athletes]]. They then simulated 1,000 seasons per sport in which injury probability depended only on the intensity of the current session, so ACWR had no effect by construction (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:43], [14:13]). In those simulations a chi-square test of ACWR against injury was "extremely highly significant" (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:43]). The apparent increase in injury risk was 6.8% for the Italian team and 10.5% for the NFL team, which the speaker says is "about of the same order" as effects reported across sports in the literature (TIRINmtZOu0 [15:15]). The talk does not say whether 6.8% and 10.5% are relative or absolute, and the numbers come from auto-captions and were not checked against the slides. They also say the first published paper, on cricket bowlers, appeared in 2014 and has been cited over 250 times, and that hundreds of papers followed (TIRINmtZOu0 [06:36], [07:07], [07:38]).
18

The simulation itself is the evidence that the pattern can arise without any ACWR effect; the speakers do not show that it did arise that way in the published studies.
20	
21	**When to apply** — When reading an ACWR injury paper or vendor claim: treat a reported ACWR effect of 5 to 10% as within what the schedule alone can produce in these two datasets. Inference: ask any vendor showing an ACWR risk curve whether it adjusts for the load of the session in which injury occurred. Eric's baseline: ACWR is looked at but not trusted for any decision, and there is no formal risk model (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit).

Their view that the products are "snake oil" is stated opinion near the start of the talk (TIRINmtZOu0 [01:01]). The simulation reproduces the association's size, not its shape: the talk does not show that the U-shape or the sweet spot (captions "08 and 1.3", probably 0.8 to 1.3, TIRINmtZOu0 [05:36]) arises from the artifact.
24

They then simulated 1,000 seasons per sport in which injury probability depended only on the intensity of the current session, so ACWR had no effect by construction (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:43], [14:13]). In those simulations a chi-square test of ACWR against injury was "extremely highly significant" (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:43]). The apparent increase in injury risk was 6.8% for the Italian team and 10.5% for the NFL team, which the speaker says is "about of the same order" as effects reported across sports in the literature (TIRINmtZOu0 [15:15]). The talk does not say whether 6.8% and 10.5% are relative or absolute, and the numbers come from auto-captions and were not checked against the slides. They also say the first published paper, on cricket bowlers, appeared in 2014 and has been cited over 250 times, and that hundreds of papers followed (TIRINmtZOu0 [06:36], [07:07], [07:38]).
18	
19	**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that a hard past week makes a hard session today likely, and today's intensity is what drives injury; see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. The simulation itself is the evidence that the pattern can arise without any ACWR effect; the speakers do not show that it did arise that way in the published studies.
20	
21	**When to apply** — When reading an ACWR injury paper or vendor claim: treat a reported ACWR effect of 5 to 10% as within what the schedule alone can produce in these two datasets. Inference: ask any vendor showing an ACWR risk curve whether it adjusts for the load of the session in which injury occurred. Eric's baseline: ACWR is looked at but not trusted for any decision, and there is no formal risk model (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit).
22	
23	**When NOT to apply** — Two teams, two sports (NFL and a European club); no stated roster size, number of injuries or load variable, so do not read 6.8% and 10.5% as a college football estimate. The speakers say they have not disproved the field and that a more complex model might still find signal (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:49], [23:35]). Their view that the products are "snake oil" is stated opinion near the start of the talk (TIRINmtZOu0 [01:01]). The simulation reproduces the association's size, not its shape: the talk does not show that the U-shape or the sweet spot (captions "08 and 1.3", probably 0.8 to 1.3, TIRINmtZOu0 [05:36]) arises from the artifact.
24	
25	**Example** — The speakers' own: NFL 10.5% and Italian soccer 6.8% apparent increase in risk from a null simulation (TIRINmtZOu0 [15:15]).

15	# Classify Chronotype, Then Time Peak Performance Relative to When the Athlete Wakes
16	
17	**What it is** — A method the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) describes from a study she attributes to a "university of Birmingham" (caption spelling) group. Competition-level athletes completed a paper-and-pencil morning-evening questionnaire, which classified them as early, intermediate or late (night owl) (J7smyg1Czik [17:22], [17:52]). Performance tests were done six times across the day: the bleep test (endurance, oxygen uptake) and sprint times, along with athletes' own ratings (J7smyg1Czik [17:52], [18:24]). As a whole group, performance was lowest at 7 am and highest in the late afternoon; the captions read "between four and seven" without am or pm (J7smyg1Czik [18:24], [18:55]). By chronotype, early types peaked between noon and 2, intermediate types in the mid-afternoon, and late types between 7 and 8 in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [18:55]). Relative to waking, early and intermediate types peaked about 6 to 7 hours after waking, and late types 11 hours or more after (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). A further analysis of a large number of athletes in 12 teams predicted team peak by team makeup: a team of mostly late types (T3) peaked later than a team of mostly early types (T10) (J7smyg1Czik [20:30], [21:00]). In the Q&A she says the body clock shifts mostly with light and can be moved with light boxes and melatonin, for example earlier bedtimes for a team trip to London, and that this takes discipline (J7smyg1Czik [29:02]).
18	
19	**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a biological clock decides whether someone is a night owl or morning lark, and everyone's peak therefore differs (J7smyg1Czik [16:51], [17:22]). Her point is that a fixed wake time, imposed by a coach or schedule, does not shift when an individual peaks (J7smyg1Czik [19:58], [20:30]). She gives no mechanism for the questionnaire's validity.
20	
21	**When to apply** — When choosing the time of day for testing or high-stakes sessions, or when comparing an athlete's results across times. Inference: record each athlete's test time and, if the staff wishes, the questionnaire result, before comparing sessions; this matters for repeatable testing. Eric's baseline (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred): testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). Eric's baseline: Eric has no stated chronotype practice; the baseline is silent.
22	
23	**When NOT to apply** — Sample sizes are not stated for the questionnaire study; the only count is 12 teams. The study is competition-level athletes, not college football, and early-morning football practice and meal schedules are not under athletes' control. The speaker says the whole circadian advantage is "unexplored" (J7smyg1Czik [23:03]). Her claim that a third of teams she talks to are not interested is her own experience (J7smyg1Czik [28:31]). A light and melatonin protocol was mentioned, not described; do not use it as a medical recommendation.
24	
25	**Example** — The speaker's own: Team 3, mostly late types, versus Team 10, mostly early types; she says if a morning game pitted them against each other, T3 would be at a biological disadvantage, and in the evening T10 would be (J7smyg1Czik [21:00], [21:32]).
26	
27	**Related** — [[claim--circadian-misalignment-shifts-game-outcomes-nfl-and-baseball]]; [[heuristic--strategic-nap-lengths-and-when-not-to-nap]].

15	# Strategic Naps: 15 to 20 Minutes, 30 Minutes or 90 Minutes, and Not When Night Sleep Is Poor
16	
17	**What it is** — In the Q&A, the speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) says nine hours in bed means nine hours over a 24-hour period, so an athlete who cannot sleep it all at once can nap (J7smyg1Czik [29:33]). She names three nap types: 15 to 20 minutes, after which you wake from light sleep and should feel refreshed; 30 minutes, which still ends in light sleep (stage two, she says); and a 90-minute "granddaddy" nap that goes through light, deep and dream sleep, after which you wake spontaneously (J7smyg1Czik [29:33], [30:03]). Her caution: if the athlete has trouble sleeping at night, a nap is "not a good thing," because it uses up the homeostatic sleep drive (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). She also says trouble falling asleep in athletes usually comes from trying to sleep at an unusual time after crossing time zones (the example is four) or from heavy caffeine in the evening because games are in the evening (J7smyg1Czik [30:35]). She adds that napping after training helps, since sleep consolidates learning and memory formed in training (J7smyg1Czik [25:25]).
18	
19	**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism for the length choice is the sleep stage you wake from: light sleep in the short naps, a full cycle in the 90-minute nap. Her caution rests on sleep drive (time awake) opposing sleep, as she describes it earlier in the talk (J7smyg1Czik [11:45], [12:48]). No study is cited for the nap lengths.
20	
21	**When to apply** — When an athlete's schedule leaves time in bed short, and nighttime sleep is otherwise good. Inference: the three lengths give a short and a long option for a travel day or a long gap between sessions. Eric's baseline: no sleep or nap protocol is in the baseline; recovery is managed through training-load design alone (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit).
22	
23	**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the nap guidance is the speaker's practical advice with no data, population or study cited. Not for athletes with poor night sleep (her own rule). The talk does not address timing relative to training or competition. Inference: a long nap close to a session may leave an athlete groggy, but the speaker does not say so. Not a substitute for a clinical sleep evaluation. Naps are a make-up for total sleep, not a replacement for regular nights, since she says deficits are cumulative (J7smyg1Czik [22:33]).
24	
25	**Example** — The speaker's own: for an athlete who cannot get nine hours in one go, split it across a night and a nap, choosing the nap length by whether the athlete will have time to wake fully (J7smyg1Czik [29:33], [30:03]).
26	
27	**Related** — [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]; [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]] (NCAA Division I nap behavior).

content.text:
All three talks are atomized: 21 entries written into `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\staging\library\sports-analytics-and-decision-making\ssac-talks--42analytics\_batch_c\`. I grep-checked that each file has all six body sections, a "When NOT to apply" section, one Related line and no em dashes outside the section headers. I did not add `_domain.md` or `_book.md`, since the prompt didn't ask for them.

**Entries by kind:** 11 claims, 5 frameworks, 4 heuristics, 1 principle.
**By confidence:** 7 supported, 13 untested, 1 contested. The contested one is `principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury`: Griffin 2020 reads the ACWR association less as an artifact, while Impellizzeri 2020 agrees with the artifact reading.

**Talks done:**
- **TIRINmtZOu0** (ACWR confounding): 6 entries.
- **K5a7C4b1Cwc** (soccer injury and selection model): 7 entries.
- **J7smyg1Czik** (science of sleep): 8 entries.

**Reciprocal-link suggestions.** These entries link to existing vault papers. Suggested back-links:
- Impellizzeri 2020 (acute-to-random) and Griffin 2020 point to the ACWR confounding principle and the null-simulation claim.
- Menaspa 2017 and the Old Bull heuristic `heuristic--rolling-baselines-miss-gradual-drift` point to the null-model framework.
- Lever 2024 (NCAA sleep and naps) points to the sleep entries.
- Vitale 2026 (sleep and jet lag consensus) points to the circadian claim.
- Lazarev 2026 (testosterone) points to the testosterone claim. It only partly conflicts: it says evidence for sleep extension as a testosterone intervention isn't established.
- Carey 2017 and Martínez-Ruiz point to the soccer injury-model and team-selection entries.

**Unclear or contradictory spots in the transcripts:**
- **ACWR talk:** The 6.8% and 10.5% risk figures are read from captions, and it isn't stated whether they are relative or absolute. The sweet spot reads "08 and 1.3" (probably 0.8 to 1.3). The Italian team is captioned "Syria" and "Serria" (probably Serie A, unconfirmed). The talk opens hostile to the industry but closes saying it didn't disprove the literature. The wellness-form remark has no named speaker.
- **Soccer talk:** The injury-cost figure is $770 million in one place and "nearly $800 million" in another. The headline 13% matches the ideal-eleven figure, not the 4.6% squad figure, and the speaker doesn't say which he means. The injury model's "five-block" cross-validation and the "VAPE" player model are garbled caption spellings. The 0.77 correlation doesn't say what was correlated.
- **Sleep talk:** The speaker is unnamed. The study design ("7 five versus 3 hours") is garbled. The injury figure "1.7%" is likely garbled and I excluded it. The football 40-yard-dash improvement is garbled. The baseball "60% or more" is unclear. The testosterone sentence reads "increased... decreased", so the direction is inferred from the next sentence. The NFL authors appear only as "Smith and motra".

**Not read:** I did not read the three `applications.md` files, so I used no Baylor application text from them. I took Eric's baseline lines only from `method-baseline.md`, not from the talks' `applications.md` files.
